FINDINGS:

The worker commit does not fail at `git checkout`. In `app/workspace.py`, `merge_worktree_to_main` asks `_branch_worktree_path` where the target branch is checked out. If another worktree owns it, Git’s worktree registry supplies that path and the merge runs there. The `git checkout <target>` step in the repository directory runs only when no worktree owns the target branch. A checkout failure there would return `cannot checkout <branch> in repo: <Git stderr>`; it would not itself produce `NO_COMMITS_MERGED`.

The raw no-op outcome is produced after the merge attempt, when the target ref is inspected again. If Git reports success but the target SHA is unchanged, `merge_worktree_to_main` sets `code=NO_COMMITS_MERGED`, `state=failed`, and `commit_point=not_reached`. `merge_worker` in `app/routes/sessions.py` also enforces this condition when it receives a nominally successful result with matching `target_before`/`target_after` and zero merged commits. So the recorded third refusal means the target ref did not change in that operation. The worker’s new commit may still exist on its branch; the result does not establish why it was not transferred.

`normalize_merge_result` in `app/merge_operations.py` preserves the no-commits classification and presents the canonical error `merge produced no new commits` with next action `CHECK_WORKER_THEN_NEW_OPERATION`. Its invariant replaces the raw error text when the target SHA is unchanged and zero commits were transferred. That user-facing message is therefore not evidence of a checkout error.

Recommendation: investigate the worker and merge preconditions to find why its commit produced no target change. Keep any fix narrowly scoped to the actual no-op cause, while preserving target-ref snapshot checks, worktree ownership handling, rollback/commit-point reporting, and the normalizer’s rule that an unchanged target with zero transferred commits cannot be reported as a successful merge.
